When penicillin became widely available in the 1940s, it transformed medicine. Infections that had once been fatal, such as pneumonia and infected wounds, could suddenly be cured within days. Yet even in those early years, scientists warned that bacteria might eventually adapt to the new drugs. That warning has proved accurate. Today, antibiotic resistance is regarded by many health organizations as one of the most serious threats to global health.

Resistance develops through a process of natural selection. In any large population of bacteria, a few individuals may carry genetic mutations that allow them to survive a particular antibiotic. When the drug is used, the vulnerable bacteria die, while the resistant ones survive and multiply. Over time, the resistant strain becomes dominant. Bacteria can also exchange genetic material with one another, so resistance that appears in one species may spread to others.

Human behaviour has greatly accelerated this process. Antibiotics are frequently prescribed for viral infections, such as the common cold, against which they have no effect. Patients often stop taking their medication as soon as they feel better, leaving the most resistant bacteria alive. In addition, large quantities of antibiotics are given to farm animals, not to treat illness but to promote faster growth.

Addressing the problem is complicated by economic factors. Developing a new antibiotic is expensive and can take more than a decade. Moreover, because doctors are encouraged to reserve new antibiotics for cases in which older drugs have failed, sales are likely to remain low. As a result, few pharmaceutical companies consider such research profitable.

Experts therefore argue that solutions must combine several approaches: more careful prescribing, stricter rules on agricultural use, better diagnostic tests and new funding models that reward companies for developing drugs even if those drugs are rarely used.

העמידות מתפתחת בתהליך של ברירה טבעית. בכל אוכלוסייה גדולה של חיידקים, מעטים עשויים לשאת מוטציות גנטיות המאפשרות להם לשרוד אנטיביוטיקה מסוימת. כאשר משתמשים בתרופה, החיידקים הפגיעים מתים, ואילו העמידים שורדים ומתרבים. עם הזמן הופך הזן העמיד לדומיננטי. חיידקים יכולים גם להחליף ביניהם חומר גנטי, כך שעמידות המופיעה במין אחד עלולה להתפשט לאחרים.

For most of human history, people measured time by natural events rather than by numbers. Farmers began work at sunrise and stopped at sunset, and the length of an hour could vary with the seasons. The spread of mechanical clocks in European towns from the fourteenth century onward gradually changed this relationship with time, although the change was far slower than is often assumed.

Early public clocks were placed in church towers and town squares, where they regulated religious services, markets and the opening of city gates. However, they were notoriously inaccurate, often gaining or losing a quarter of an hour each day. For centuries, therefore, they served more as symbols of civic pride than as precise instruments.

The decisive shift came with industrialization in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Factory owners needed large numbers of workers to arrive at the same time and to work fixed shifts, since machines could not run efficiently otherwise. Workers who had previously controlled the pace of their own labour were now paid by the hour and fined for lateness. Some historians argue that this represented not merely a technical change but a profound transformation in how people thought about their lives: time became something to be spent, saved or wasted.

The railway completed this process. Before trains, each town kept its own local time, based on the position of the sun. A difference of a few minutes between neighbouring towns hardly mattered when travel was slow. Once trains ran according to timetables, however, such differences caused confusion and even accidents. Railway companies consequently adopted standard times, and governments eventually followed their example.

Today, when phones display the time to the second, it is easy to forget that the precise, uniform time we take for granted is a relatively recent invention.

Imagine being asked whether the population of a certain city is more or less than five million, and then being asked to estimate the actual figure. Research in psychology suggests that your estimate would be strongly influenced by the number you heard first, even if you knew that number had been chosen at random. This tendency, known as the anchoring effect, is one of the most robust findings in the study of human judgment.

In classic experiments, participants were shown a random number, for example by spinning a wheel, before answering a factual question. Those who saw a high number consistently gave higher estimates than those who saw a low one. Remarkably, the effect appeared even among experts. In one study, experienced judges who read a case and were given an arbitrary sentencing suggestion recommended longer sentences when the suggestion was high.

Why does anchoring occur? One explanation is that people start from the initial number and adjust away from it, but they tend to stop adjusting too soon. Another is that the anchor brings to mind information consistent with it, making certain answers seem more plausible.

The effect has obvious commercial applications. Shops often display a high original price next to a sale price, making the discounted product appear to be a bargain. Similarly, in salary negotiations, the first figure mentioned frequently shapes the final agreement, which is why negotiators are sometimes advised to make the first offer.

Can people protect themselves against anchoring? Simply being aware of the effect appears to help only slightly. A more effective strategy may be to consider deliberately why the anchor might be wrong, or to form one's own estimate before encountering any figures. Even so, researchers caution that no technique eliminates the bias entirely.

Plastic was once celebrated as a miracle material: cheap, light, durable and endlessly adaptable. Its durability, however, has turned out to be a serious problem. Most plastics do not biodegrade in any meaningful sense. Instead, exposed to sunlight, waves and friction, they break down into ever smaller fragments. Pieces smaller than five millimetres are known as microplastics, and they have now been detected almost everywhere scientists have looked, from deep ocean trenches to Arctic snow.

Microplastics come from two main sources. Some are manufactured at a small size, such as the tiny beads once common in cosmetic scrubs; many countries have since banned these products. Far more, however, result from the breakdown of larger items, including bottles, bags and fishing nets. Synthetic clothing is another significant source, as fibres are released every time such garments are washed.

The environmental effects are still being investigated. Marine animals, from plankton to whales, swallow microplastics, which may cause physical damage or reduce their ability to absorb nutrients. There is also concern that the particles can carry harmful chemicals, either additives used in manufacturing or pollutants that attach to their surface in the water.

Whether microplastics pose a direct threat to human health remains uncertain. They have been found in drinking water, seafood and even human blood, but researchers have not yet established what levels, if any, are dangerous. Part of the difficulty is methodological: the particles vary enormously in size, shape and chemical composition, and samples are easily contaminated by plastic in the laboratory itself.

Because removing microplastics from the environment is practically impossible, most experts agree that the only realistic approach is to prevent them from forming in the first place. This means reducing plastic production, improving waste management and designing products that shed fewer fibres.

עדיין לא ברור אם מיקרופלסטיק מהווה איום ישיר על בריאות האדם. הוא נמצא במי שתייה, במאכלי ים ואפילו בדם האדם, אך החוקרים טרם קבעו אילו רמות, אם בכלל, מסוכנות. חלק מהקושי הוא מתודולוגי: החלקיקים שונים מאוד זה מזה בגודל, בצורה ובהרכב הכימי, ודגימות מזדהמות בקלות מפלסטיק שנמצא במעבדה עצמה.

מאחר שסילוק מיקרופלסטיק מהסביבה הוא כמעט בלתי אפשרי, רוב המומחים מסכימים שהגישה המציאותית היחידה היא למנוע את היווצרותו מלכתחילה. משמעות הדבר היא צמצום ייצור הפלסטיק, שיפור הטיפול בפסולת ותכנון מוצרים שמשחררים פחות סיבים.

Young children learning English often say things like I goed to the park or two mouses, forms they have almost certainly never heard from adults. At first glance, these errors might seem to show that the child's language is getting worse. In fact, linguists regard them as evidence of an important step in language development.

Interestingly, many children first use irregular forms such as went and mice correctly. At this early stage, they appear to memorize each word as a separate item. Later, as they hear more and more regular forms such as walked and cats, they begin to extract the underlying rule: add -ed to form the past tense, add -s to form the plural. Having discovered the rule, they then apply it too widely, a process known as overregularization. Only gradually do they learn which words are exceptions, and the correct irregular forms return.

This U-shaped pattern, in which performance first improves, then declines, and finally improves again, has been influential in debates about how language is acquired. If children simply imitated what they heard, they would never produce forms like goed. The errors therefore suggest that children are actively constructing a grammatical system rather than merely copying adults.

Not all researchers interpret the evidence in the same way, however. Some argue that children do not learn abstract rules at all but rely on statistical patterns in the language they hear; according to this view, overregularization occurs because regular forms are far more frequent. Computer models based on this idea have reproduced some aspects of children's errors, although their success remains debated.

Whatever the explanation, one practical conclusion is widely accepted: parents need not worry about such mistakes. Correcting them repeatedly has little effect, and they usually disappear on their own as the child's experience with language grows.

Every time a person watches a video, clicks on a news article or buys a product online, a recommendation system records the choice and uses it to suggest what to show next. These systems, which rely on algorithms that identify patterns in the behaviour of millions of users, have become central to the business of many technology companies. Their purpose is straightforward: to keep users engaged for as long as possible.

Critics have argued that this approach may have unintended social consequences. If algorithms show people only content similar to what they have previously chosen, users may become trapped in a filter bubble, exposed mainly to views that confirm their existing beliefs. Over time, it is claimed, this could deepen political divisions and make it harder for citizens to agree on basic facts.

The empirical evidence, however, is more mixed than this picture suggests. Several large studies have found that most users encounter a wider range of sources online than the bubble theory predicts, partly because social networks connect them with acquaintances whose views differ from their own. Other research indicates that people's own choices, rather than algorithms, are the main reason they consume one-sided content. In other words, the bubble may be built less by the machine than by its users.

This does not mean that recommendation systems are harmless. There is evidence that content provoking strong emotions, particularly anger, tends to attract more engagement and is therefore promoted more widely. Even if algorithms do not isolate users completely, they may still reward sensational or misleading material.

Proposed responses range from greater transparency, allowing independent researchers to examine how algorithms work, to giving users more control over what they see. Each approach, however, raises its own difficulties, from the need to protect commercial secrets to the observation that many users rarely change default settings.

בכל פעם שאדם צופה בסרטון, לוחץ על כתבה חדשותית או קונה מוצר ברשת, מערכת המלצות מתעדת את הבחירה ומשתמשת בה כדי להציע מה להציג בהמשך. מערכות אלה, הנשענות על אלגוריתמים המזהים דפוסים בהתנהגותם של מיליוני משתמשים, הפכו למרכזיות בעסקיהן של חברות טכנולוגיה רבות. מטרתן פשוטה: להשאיר את המשתמשים מעורבים זמן רב ככל האפשר.

אולם הראיות האמפיריות מעורבות יותר משתמונה זו מרמזת. כמה מחקרים גדולים מצאו שרוב המשתמשים נחשפים ברשת למגוון רחב יותר של מקורות ממה שתיאוריית הבועה צופה, בין היתר משום שרשתות חברתיות מחברות אותם למכרים שדעותיהם שונות משלהם. מחקרים אחרים מראים שהבחירות של האנשים עצמם, ולא האלגוריתמים, הן הסיבה העיקרית לכך שהם צורכים תוכן חד-צדדי. במילים אחרות, ייתכן שאת הבועה בונה לא כל כך המכונה אלא דווקא המשתמשים בה.

אין פירוש הדבר שמערכות ההמלצה אינן מזיקות. יש ראיות לכך שתוכן המעורר רגשות עזים, במיוחד כעס, נוטה למשוך יותר מעורבות ולכן מקודם באופן נרחב יותר. גם אם האלגוריתמים אינם מבודדים את המשתמשים לחלוטין, הם עדיין עשויים לתגמל חומר סנסציוני או מטעה.

When a resource is shared by many people but owned by none, each individual has an incentive to use as much of it as possible. A fisherman who limits his catch to protect fish stocks bears the full cost of his restraint, while the benefits are shared by all, including competitors who continue to fish freely. If everyone reasons in this way, the resource may be exhausted, even though no one wanted this outcome. Economists call this situation the tragedy of the commons.

For many years, the standard solutions were either government regulation or private ownership. Governments could set limits on fishing or grazing and punish those who exceeded them; alternatively, the resource could be divided among private owners, each of whom would have a direct interest in its long-term health.

Later research, however, challenged the assumption that these were the only options. Studies of communities around the world, from mountain villages managing shared pastures to coastal groups controlling local fisheries, revealed that many had sustained common resources for centuries without either outside regulation or privatization. These communities had developed their own rules, monitored one another's behaviour and imposed gradually increasing penalties on those who broke the rules.

Such arrangements tended to succeed under particular conditions. The group of users was usually clearly defined, members could communicate easily, and the people who followed the rules had a say in making them. Where these conditions were absent, for instance where users were numerous, anonymous or constantly changing, self-governance was far less likely to work.

The lesson is not that regulation and markets are unnecessary, but that they are not the only tools available. For problems such as climate change, which involve billions of people, cooperation remains enormously difficult. Yet the experience of local communities shows that the tragedy of the commons is a risk rather than an inevitability.

כאשר משאב משותף לאנשים רבים אך אינו שייך לאף אחד, לכל יחיד יש תמריץ לנצל ממנו כמה שיותר. דייג המגביל את שללו כדי להגן על אוכלוסיית הדגים נושא במלוא העלות של האיפוק שלו, ואילו התועלת מתחלקת בין כולם, כולל מתחרים הממשיכים לדוג בחופשיות. אם כולם חושבים כך, המשאב עלול להתכלות, אף שאיש לא רצה בתוצאה זו. כלכלנים מכנים מצב זה טרגדיית נחלת הכלל.

במשך שנים רבות, הפתרונות המקובלים היו רגולציה ממשלתית או בעלות פרטית. ממשלות יכלו לקבוע מגבלות על דיג או על רעייה ולהעניש את מי שחרג מהן; לחלופין, אפשר היה לחלק את המשאב בין בעלים פרטיים, שלכל אחד מהם יהיה אינטרס ישיר בשמירה על המשאב לאורך זמן.

אולם מחקרים מאוחרים יותר ערערו על ההנחה שאלה האפשרויות היחידות. מחקרים על קהילות ברחבי העולם, מכפרי הרים המנהלים שטחי מרעה משותפים ועד לקבוצות בחוף השולטות בדיג המקומי, גילו שרבות מהן שמרו על משאבים משותפים במשך מאות שנים בלי רגולציה חיצונית ובלי הפרטה. קהילות אלה פיתחו כללים משלהן, פיקחו זו על התנהגותו של זה והטילו עונשים שהלכו והחמירו על מי שהפר את הכללים.

הסדרים כאלה נטו להצליח בתנאים מסוימים. קבוצת המשתמשים הייתה בדרך כלל מוגדרת בבירור, החברים יכלו לתקשר בקלות, ולמי שציית לכללים הייתה השפעה על קביעתם. במקומות שבהם תנאים אלה לא התקיימו, למשל כאשר המשתמשים היו רבים, אנונימיים או מתחלפים כל הזמן, הסיכוי שניהול עצמי יצליח היה נמוך בהרבה.

הלקח אינו שרגולציה ושווקים מיותרים, אלא שהם אינם הכלים היחידים העומדים לרשותנו. בבעיות כמו שינויי האקלים, המערבות מיליארדי בני אדם, שיתוף פעולה עדיין קשה מאוד. ובכל זאת, ניסיונן של קהילות מקומיות מראה שטרגדיית נחלת הכלל היא סיכון ולא גזירת גורל.

When people think of intelligent animals, they usually picture apes, dolphins or perhaps crows. Few would think of the octopus, a creature more closely related to snails and clams than to any vertebrate. Yet a growing body of research indicates that octopuses possess remarkable cognitive abilities, and their intelligence raises intriguing questions about how minds evolve.

In laboratory settings, octopuses have learned to open screw-top jars, find their way through mazes and distinguish between different shapes. Some have been observed escaping from their tanks at night and returning before morning. In the wild, certain species collect coconut shells and carry them across the sea floor for later use as shelters, behaviour that some researchers consider a form of tool use.

What makes these abilities especially striking is the octopus's unusual nervous system. Of its roughly 500 million neurons, about two thirds are located not in the brain but in the arms. Each arm can, to a considerable degree, sense and respond to its environment independently, so that an arm may continue to search for food even when the animal's attention appears to be elsewhere. This arrangement differs fundamentally from the centralized nervous systems of mammals and birds.

Because the last common ancestor of octopuses and humans lived more than 500 million years ago and was probably a simple worm-like animal, complex intelligence must have evolved separately in the two lineages. This suggests that there may be more than one evolutionary route to a sophisticated mind.

Octopus intelligence is all the more puzzling given the animal's short life. Most species live only one or two years and have little contact with their parents, so they cannot learn from older generations. Why such a short-lived, solitary animal should develop such abilities remains an open question, though some scientists point to the demands of hunting in complex environments while avoiding predators without the protection of a shell.

כשאנשים חושבים על בעלי חיים נבונים, הם מדמיינים בדרך כלל קופי אדם, דולפינים או אולי עורבים. מעטים יחשבו על התמנון, יצור הקרוב יותר לחלזונות ולצדפות מאשר לבעל חוליות כלשהו. אולם גוף מחקר הולך וגדל מראה שלתמנונים יכולות קוגניטיביות מרשימות, והאינטליגנציה שלהם מעוררת שאלות מסקרנות על האופן שבו מתפתחת תודעה.

בתנאי מעבדה למדו תמנונים לפתוח צנצנות עם מכסה מתברג, למצוא את דרכם במבוכים ולהבחין בין צורות שונות. חלקם נצפו בורחים מהאקווריום שלהם בלילה וחוזרים לפני הבוקר. בטבע, מינים מסוימים אוספים קליפות קוקוס ונושאים אותן על פני קרקעית הים כדי להשתמש בהן מאוחר יותר כמחסה, התנהגות שחלק מהחוקרים רואים בה סוג של שימוש בכלים.

מה שהופך יכולות אלה למרשימות במיוחד היא מערכת העצבים יוצאת הדופן של התמנון. מתוך כחמש מאות מיליון תאי העצב שלו, כשני שלישים נמצאים לא במוח אלא בזרועות. כל זרוע יכולה, במידה ניכרת, לחוש את סביבתה ולהגיב אליה באופן עצמאי, כך שזרוע עשויה להמשיך לחפש מזון גם כאשר נראה שתשומת הלב של בעל החיים נתונה למקום אחר. מבנה זה שונה באופן יסודי ממערכות העצבים הריכוזיות של יונקים ועופות.

מאחר שהאב הקדמון המשותף האחרון של התמנונים ובני האדם חי לפני יותר מחמש מאות מיליון שנה והיה ככל הנראה בעל חיים פשוט דמוי תולעת, אינטליגנציה מורכבת חייבת הייתה להתפתח בנפרד בשני הענפים. הדבר מרמז שייתכן שיש יותר מדרך אבולוציונית אחת לתודעה מתוחכמת.

האינטליגנציה של התמנון מעוררת תמיהה רבה עוד יותר לנוכח חייו הקצרים. רוב המינים חיים שנה או שנתיים בלבד ויש להם מגע מועט עם הוריהם, ולכן אינם יכולים ללמוד מדורות קודמים. השאלה מדוע בעל חיים קצר ימים ובודד כזה פיתח יכולות כאלה נותרה פתוחה, אף שיש מדענים המצביעים על הדרישות של ציד בסביבות מורכבות תוך התחמקות מטורפים ללא הגנה של קונכייה.

Every spring, hundreds of people run through the streets of Haifa in a special race. The runners do not try to win prizes. Instead, each runner asks friends and family to donate money for every kilometer they finish. This year, the money went to a center for children with serious illnesses.

Maya, sixteen, decided to take part after her younger cousin spent a month in hospital. She had never run more than two kilometers before, so she started training three months early. Every morning before school, she ran in the park near her home. Some days it rained and she wanted to stay in bed, but she remembered her cousin and went out anyway.

He explained that the crater was not made by a meteor, as many people believe, but by water and wind over millions of years. In the afternoon, they saw a group of ibex, wild goats with long, curved horns, standing calmly near the road.

At night, the family went outside to look at the sky. Because there are very few lights in the area, they could see thousands of stars. Bamba is not an ordinary dog. Every Tuesday, she visits a home for elderly people in Rishon LeZion together with her owner, Dana, who is a volunteer. Bamba is a therapy dog. This means she has been trained to stay calm around strangers, noise and wheelchairs.

When Bamba enters the room, the residents' faces change. Some of them, who usually sit alone and say very little, begin to smile and talk. They stroke her soft fur and tell Dana about the dogs they had when they were young. One man, who rarely leaves his room, now waits by the door every Tuesday.

Scientists have found that spending time with animals can lower stress and make people feel less lonely. However, not every dog can do this job. Training takes about a year, and the dog must pass a test. Dana says that Bamba enjoys the visits as much as the residents do.

Some of the world's most useful inventions started with a simple walk. In the 1940s, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral went hiking in the mountains with his dog. When they came home, he noticed small burrs, the seeds of a plant, stuck to his trousers and to the dog's fur.

Most people would just remove them and forget about it. But de Mestral was curious. He looked at the burrs under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks. These hooks caught on anything with loops, like cloth or hair.

He wondered if he could copy this idea to make a new kind of fastener. It took him many years of experiments, because at first the material broke too easily. Finally, he succeeded, and he called his invention Velcro.

At first, fashion companies were not interested. Later, astronauts used Velcro in space, and soon it appeared on shoes, bags and jackets all over the world.

רוב האנשים פשוט היו מורידים אותם ושוכחים מזה. אבל דה מסטרל היה סקרן. הוא הסתכל על הזרעים במיקרוסקופ וראה מאות ווים זעירים. הווים האלה נתפסו בכל דבר שיש בו לולאות, כמו בד או שיער.

בהתחלה חברות אופנה לא התעניינו. מאוחר יותר אסטרונאוטים השתמשו בוולקרו בחלל, ומהר מאוד הוא הופיע על נעליים, תיקים ומעילים בכל העולם.

Many teenagers go to bed late and find it very hard to wake up in the morning. Parents often think this is just laziness, but scientists say there is a biological reason.

During the teenage years, the body produces melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, later in the evening than it does in children or adults. As a result, many teens do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or even later. However, school still starts early, so they often sleep only six or seven hours a night. Experts say teenagers need between eight and ten hours.

Lack of sleep can cause serious problems. Tired students find it harder to concentrate, remember information and control their mood. They are also more likely to get sick.

Teenagers may be especially sensitive. In one experiment, young participants were shown photos that had either many or few likes. Some platforms have responded by allowing users to hide the number of likes on their posts. Early reports indicate that this reduces pressure for some users, although others say they miss the feedback.

Experts do not recommend abandoning social media altogether. Instead, they suggest using it more consciously: turning off notifications, setting time limits and remembering that the value of a post, or of a person, is not measured by a number.

Long before telephones and the internet, people needed fast ways to send important messages. One of the most reliable solutions was surprisingly simple: the homing pigeon.

Homing pigeons have an extraordinary ability to find their way back to their home loft, even when they are released hundreds of kilometres away. Scientists are still not completely sure how they do it. Some believe the birds use the position of the sun, while others think they can sense the Earth's magnetic field. Most likely, they combine several methods.

Ancient civilisations were already aware of this talent. Pigeons were used to announce the results of sporting competitions and to carry news between cities. Centuries later, businesses used them to deliver financial information faster than horses could.

Pigeons proved most valuable, however, during wartime. When telephone lines were cut and radio signals could be intercepted by the enemy, small messages were tied to the birds' legs. Many pigeons were shot down or lost in storms, but enough of them arrived to save thousands of lives. Several birds were even given medals for bravery.

Today, pigeons are rarely used for communication, but the sport of pigeon racing remains popular in some countries, where owners train their birds for years. Their story is a reminder that sometimes the most effective technology is the one that nature has already invented.

Ask a group of teenagers what they want to be when they grow up, and you may hear answers that would have confused people fifty years ago: drone pilot, app developer, data scientist, social media manager. None of these professions existed in their current form when today's grandparents were choosing their careers.

Technology is the main reason for this change. As new tools are invented, new kinds of work appear around them. At the same time, some older jobs, such as telephone operators and typists, have almost disappeared. Experts predict that this process will speed up in the coming decades, especially as artificial intelligence takes over routine tasks.

This creates a challenge for schools. How can teachers prepare students for jobs that do not exist yet? Many educators believe the answer is to focus less on memorising facts and more on skills that can be used in any field. These include critical thinking, creativity, teamwork and the ability to keep learning throughout life.

Career counsellors also advise young people not to worry too much about choosing the "perfect" profession at eighteen. Most adults today change careers several times. Daniel, a 34-year-old who studied history and now designs video games, says his first degree was not wasted. "History taught me how to tell a story," he explains. "That's exactly what a good game needs."

In almost every sport, from football to basketball, teams win more often when they play in their own stadium. This phenomenon, known as "home advantage", has been recorded for over a century. But what exactly causes it?

For a long time, many fans believed that the noise of the crowd gave home players extra energy. While this may be part of the explanation, researchers have discovered that the crowd might affect referees even more than players. In one study, experienced referees watched videos of football fouls. Half of them watched with the sound of a loud crowd, and half watched in silence. Those who heard the crowd gave fewer fouls against the home team.

Other factors also seem to matter. Visiting teams often have to travel long distances, which can cause tiredness. Home players are familiar with their own field, the weather and even the local food. They also sleep in their own beds before a game.

An unusual opportunity to test these ideas came when many matches were played in empty stadiums during the COVID-19 pandemic. Without fans, home advantage became noticeably smaller in several leagues, and referees' decisions became more balanced. This supported the theory that crowds play an important role.

Still, home advantage has not disappeared completely, which suggests that travel and familiarity continue to make a difference.

Yogurt, cheese, bread, pickles and soy sauce may seem to have little in common. Yet they all depend on the same natural process: fermentation. In fermentation, tiny living organisms such as bacteria and yeast break down sugars in food, changing its taste, texture and smell.

Humans have been fermenting food for thousands of years, long before anyone knew that microorganisms existed. In the past, fermentation was mainly a way to preserve food. Without refrigerators, fresh milk or vegetables would spoil within days. Once fermented, however, they could last for weeks or even months. This allowed communities to survive long winters and periods of poor harvest.

Every culture developed its own fermented foods, often based on local ingredients. Korean kimchi is made from cabbage and spices, while Eastern European families traditionally pickled cucumbers in salty water. In the Middle East, people have long enjoyed labneh, a thick yogurt cheese.

In recent years, fermentation has become fashionable again. Some researchers believe that certain fermented foods may support healthy digestion, since they contain helpful bacteria. However, scientists warn that more studies are needed before strong claims can be made, and that not all products sold in supermarkets contain live bacteria.

For many home cooks, the attraction is simpler. Making your own pickles is cheap, creative and connects you to generations of people who did exactly the same.

בשנים האחרונות, התסיסה חזרה להיות אופנתית. יש חוקרים הסבורים שמזונות מותססים מסוימים עשויים לתמוך בעיכול בריא, משום שהם מכילים חיידקים מועילים. עם זאת, מדענים מזהירים שנדרשים מחקרים נוספים לפני שאפשר יהיה לטעון טענות חד־משמעיות, ושלא כל המוצרים הנמכרים בסופרמרקטים מכילים חיידקים חיים.

For many tourists, a holiday means visiting as many places as possible in the shortest time. They rush from one famous site to the next, take hundreds of photos and return home more exhausted than when they left. A growing movement known as "slow travel" suggests a different approach.

Slow travellers choose to stay longer in fewer places. Rather than seeing five cities in a week, they might spend the entire week in one small town. They rent an apartment instead of staying in a hotel, shop at local markets and try to learn a few words of the local language. The goal is not to collect destinations but to experience daily life in a new place.

Supporters argue that this style of travel has several advantages. It is often cheaper, because long-term rentals cost less per night and travellers spend less on transport. It is also better for the environment, especially when people take trains instead of short flights. Perhaps most importantly, it allows for real connections with local people.

Critics point out that not everyone has the time or freedom to travel slowly. Many workers receive only a few days of vacation each year. Even so, the principles can be applied to shorter trips as well. Choosing one neighbourhood to explore deeply, rather than racing across a city, can turn an ordinary weekend into a memorable experience.

When a honeybee discovers a field full of flowers, it faces a problem: how can it tell the other bees in the hive where to find the food? Bees cannot speak, yet they have developed one of the most remarkable communication systems in the animal world.

Back in the hive, the bee performs a special movement known as the "waggle dance". It walks in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. Researchers discovered in the twentieth century that this dance contains precise information. The direction of the straight line shows the direction of the flowers in relation to the sun. The length of the waggle tells the other bees how far away the food is.

Other bees gather around the dancer, follow its movements and then fly directly to the right place, sometimes several kilometres away. The discovery was so surprising that many scientists did not believe it at first. It took years of careful experiments before the idea was widely accepted.

Today, researchers study the waggle dance for practical reasons as well. By "reading" the dances, they can learn which areas provide bees with food. This information helps farmers and environmental groups protect bee populations, which have declined in many parts of the world. Since bees pollinate a large part of the crops we eat, their survival matters to us all.

כאשר דבורת דבש מגלה שדה מלא פרחים, היא ניצבת בפני בעיה: כיצד תוכל לספר לדבורים האחרות בכוורת היכן למצוא את המזון? דבורים אינן יכולות לדבר, ובכל זאת הן פיתחו את אחת ממערכות התקשורת המדהימות ביותר בעולם החי.

For decades, doctors have assumed that a placebo works only when the patient is deceived. A sugar pill, the reasoning goes, can relieve pain or anxiety because the person swallowing it believes it contains real medicine. Remove the belief, and the effect should disappear. In recent years, however, a small but growing body of research has challenged this assumption in a surprising way.

In several trials, researchers gave patients pills that were openly labelled as placebos. The participants, who suffered from conditions such as chronic back pain and irritable bowel syndrome, were told plainly that the capsules contained no active ingredient. They were also told that placebos had produced improvements in earlier studies, possibly through the body's automatic responses to the ritual of taking medicine. To the surprise of many, a significant number of these patients reported less pain and better daily functioning than a comparison group that received no pills at all.

How can this be explained? One theory holds that the act of treatment itself, the visit to a caring professional and the routine of swallowing a pill twice a day, triggers expectations that the brain cannot simply switch off. Even when we know a pill is empty, years of experience have taught our bodies to associate medicine with relief.

Critics urge caution. Most of the studies have been small, and the improvements were measured largely through patients' own reports rather than objective tests. Pain is real, they argue, but so is the desire to please researchers who have been kind to you.

Nevertheless, the findings raise an intriguing ethical possibility. If placebos can help without deception, doctors may one day prescribe them honestly, avoiding the moral problem that has always surrounded their use. Such a development would not replace conventional treatment, but it might remind medicine that healing involves more than chemistry.

Imagine being able to reach almost everything you need, from a grocery store and a school to a doctor and a park, within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride from your home. This is the central idea behind the 'fifteen-minute city', an approach to urban planning that has attracted the attention of mayors and architects around the world.

For much of the twentieth century, cities were designed around the private car. Planners separated neighbourhoods by function: people lived in one area, worked in another and shopped in a third, connected by wide roads and highways. This model promised freedom and efficiency, but it also produced traffic jams, air pollution and long daily commutes that consumed hours of people's lives.

Supporters of the fifteen-minute city argue that bringing services closer to residents would reverse these problems. Fewer car journeys would mean cleaner air and quieter streets. Local shops would benefit from regular customers, and neighbours who meet on the pavement rather than behind windscreens might develop a stronger sense of community. Some cities have already begun experimenting, turning parking spaces into small gardens and opening school playgrounds to the public after hours.

The idea, however, has not been universally welcomed. Some critics worry that it could increase inequality: wealthy districts may quickly attract new cafés and clinics, while poorer areas are left behind. Others fear that the concept could be used to justify restrictions on driving, which they see as an attack on personal freedom. Planners respond that the goal is to offer choices, not to impose limits.

What is clear is that the debate touches on a deeper question: what is a city for? If the answer is simply moving people and goods quickly, the car-centred model may suffice. If it is about how people live together, the fifteen-minute city deserves serious consideration.

Human memory is famously unreliable. We forget names, misplace keys and reshape our recollections each time we recall them. For a long time this was seen purely as a weakness. Yet some psychologists now argue that forgetting is not a failure of memory but one of its essential functions. It allows us to move past embarrassment, to forgive, and to become different people from who we once were.

Digital technology has changed this balance. A comment written carelessly at sixteen may remain searchable for decades. Photographs, messages and location records are stored on distant servers, often long after their owners have forgotten them. In effect, we have built a world that remembers everything and rarely lets us forget.

This raises difficult ethical questions. Should a person have the right to have old information about them removed from search results? Some legal systems have answered yes, at least in certain cases, allowing individuals to request that outdated or irrelevant links be hidden. Supporters claim that this protects dignity and gives people a genuine second chance.

Opponents, on the other hand, warn of serious risks. If anyone can erase unflattering records, they argue, the powerful might use such laws to bury evidence of wrongdoing. Journalists and historians depend on access to the past; a society that deletes too readily may lose the ability to hold its leaders accountable.

Perhaps the solution lies not in choosing between total memory and total forgetting but in designing systems that age information, much as the human mind does. Data could gradually become less visible over time unless there is a clear public interest in keeping it prominent. Such an approach would not be simple to implement. Still, it would reflect an important insight: a healthy memory, whether human or digital, depends as much on what it lets go as on what it keeps.

If you were asked to describe where a cup is on a table, you would probably say it is 'to the left' of the plate or 'in front of' you. These descriptions depend on the position of your own body. Surprisingly, not all languages work this way. Speakers of a number of languages around the world rarely use words like 'left' and 'right'. Instead, they describe locations using fixed directions such as north, south, east and west, even indoors and even for small objects. In such a language, one might say, 'There is an ant on your southern leg.'

Linguists who have studied these communities report a remarkable consequence. Speakers of these languages tend to know which way they are facing at all times, even in unfamiliar buildings or after travelling in the dark. Children learn this skill early, because without it they simply cannot speak correctly. For them, a constant awareness of direction is not a special talent but an ordinary part of daily life.

Findings like these have revived an old debate. Does the language we speak shape the way we think, or does it merely reflect it? The strong version of the claim, that language determines thought and that we cannot think what we cannot say, has largely been rejected. Speakers of every language can learn new concepts, after all. A weaker version, however, enjoys considerable support: the habits our language demands may train our attention in particular directions.

This weaker view suggests that learning a foreign language involves more than memorising vocabulary. It may also mean practising a new way of noticing the world. Whether that changes who we are is open to question, but it certainly makes the experience of learning languages richer than a list of words might suggest.

Today it seems obvious that everyone in a country should share the same time. Yet until the second half of the nineteenth century, most towns kept their own local time, based on the position of the sun. When the sun stood highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, a town only a short distance to the west would reach noon a few minutes later than its neighbour. For centuries, this caused few problems. Travel was slow, and a difference of several minutes hardly mattered to someone arriving by horse.

The railway changed everything. Trains could cover in hours distances that had once taken days, and timetables had to be precise. With dozens of local times in use, a single journey might involve several clocks showing different hours. Passengers missed connections, and, more seriously, the confusion increased the risk of collisions on shared tracks.

Railway companies were the first to act. They adopted a standard time along their lines, usually based on the clock of a major city. At first, many communities resisted. Some residents felt that abandoning 'sun time' meant surrendering a local tradition to distant business interests. In certain towns, public clocks were fitted with two minute hands, one showing local time and the other railway time.

Eventually, however, practical needs prevailed. Governments formally adopted standard time, and international agreements later divided the world into time zones. What had begun as a solution to a technical problem became a basic structure of modern life.

The story is a reminder that many arrangements we take for granted were once controversial. Even something as seemingly natural as the time on our watches is, in fact, the result of human decisions, negotiation and compromise.

Have you ever noticed that coffee shops often offer three cup sizes, and that the medium one seems like the obvious choice? This is rarely an accident. Economists who study consumer behaviour have shown that our decisions are strongly influenced by the options placed beside the one we eventually choose.

Consider a well-known kind of experiment. Participants are offered a subscription to a magazine in one of two forms: online only, for a low price, or print plus online, for a much higher price. Most people choose the cheaper option. Then researchers add a third choice: print only, at exactly the same high price as print plus online. Hardly anyone selects this new option, since it is clearly worse value. Yet its presence changes everything. Suddenly, a large majority of participants choose the expensive combined package.

The third option is known as a 'decoy'. It exists not to be bought but to make another product look attractive by comparison. Because people find it difficult to judge value in absolute terms, they rely on relative comparisons. When one option is obviously superior to a similar alternative, it appears to be a bargain, even if we would not have chosen it otherwise.

Decoys are used widely, from restaurant menus, where a very expensive dish makes other dishes seem reasonable, to electronics stores and holiday packages. Some critics consider the practice manipulative, arguing that it exploits weaknesses in human reasoning. Businesses reply that they are simply presenting choices and that customers remain free to decide.

Either way, awareness is the consumer's best defence. Before choosing, it is worth asking a simple question: would I still want this option if the others were not there? The answer may save more money than any discount.

When a famous painting is cleaned and restored, the result is often celebrated as a rediscovery. Colours that had been hidden for centuries under layers of dirt and yellowed varnish suddenly glow again, and viewers feel they are seeing the work as the artist intended. Yet restoration is one of the most controversial activities in the art world, and every major project tends to divide experts.

The central difficulty is that no one can be entirely sure what the artist intended. Paintings change over time in ways that are not always reversible. Pigments fade or darken, and earlier restorers may have added paint of their own. When a conservator removes a layer, there is a risk of removing something the artist placed there deliberately, such as a thin glaze designed to soften a bright colour. Once removed, such details cannot be recovered.

For this reason, many modern conservators follow a principle of minimal intervention. They aim to stabilise a work and protect it from further damage rather than to make it look new. Any additions they make are designed to be reversible, so that future experts, with better tools and knowledge, can undo them.

Others argue that this cautious approach goes too far. A painting covered in grime, they say, cannot communicate with its audience. If careful research shows what the original surface looked like, conservators have a duty to reveal it.

Perhaps the debate cannot be fully resolved, because it reflects a deeper uncertainty about what a work of art really is. Is it the object as it left the artist's studio, or the object as it exists now, including the marks that time has left on it? Each answer leads to a different idea of what it means to care for the past.

For most of human history, a clear night revealed thousands of stars. Today, a large proportion of the world's population lives under skies so bright that the Milky Way is no longer visible. Artificial light, which has transformed human life in countless positive ways, has also produced a form of pollution that is easy to overlook precisely because it seems so harmless.

Scientists, however, are increasingly concerned about its effects. Many animals depend on darkness. Sea turtle hatchlings, for instance, find their way to the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, which naturally lies over the water. Near brightly lit coastal roads, they may crawl inland instead, where few survive. Migrating birds can become disoriented by illuminated buildings, and insects that are drawn to street lamps often die of exhaustion, with consequences for the plants and animals that depend on them.

Humans are affected too. Our bodies follow a daily rhythm regulated partly by light and darkness. Exposure to bright light late in the evening can disturb sleep, and some researchers suspect that long-term disruption may contribute to a range of health problems, though the evidence is still being gathered.

Unlike many environmental problems, light pollution could be reduced relatively quickly and cheaply. Shielding lamps so that they shine downwards rather than into the sky, using warmer colours, and dimming or switching off lights when they are not needed would all make a significant difference. Several towns that have adopted such measures report lower energy bills as well as darker skies.

The challenge is largely one of awareness. Few people think of a lit street as a source of pollution. Yet once we recognise what has been lost, the return of a starry sky may become not merely a scientific goal but a cultural one.

במשך רוב ההיסטוריה האנושית, לילה בהיר חשף אלפי כוכבים. כיום, חלק גדול מאוכלוסיית העולם חי תחת שמיים מוארים כל כך שכבר אי אפשר לראות את שביל החלב. האור המלאכותי, ששינה את חיי האדם בדרכים חיוביות רבות מספור, יצר גם סוג של זיהום שקל להתעלם ממנו בדיוק משום שהוא נראה כה בלתי מזיק.

Since the first artificial satellite was launched in the 1950s, humans have sent thousands of objects into orbit around the Earth. Satellites now support weather forecasting, navigation, communication and scientific research. But space around our planet is becoming crowded, and much of what is up there is no longer useful.

Experts use the term 'space debris' to describe dead satellites, discarded rocket parts and countless fragments created when objects break apart or collide. Even a tiny fragment can be dangerous. Because objects in orbit travel at extraordinary speeds, many times faster than a bullet, a piece of metal the size of a coin can strike with the force of an explosion. Spacecraft carrying astronauts must sometimes change course to avoid such pieces.

The greatest fear is a chain reaction. If two large objects collide, they may produce thousands of new fragments, each of which could hit other satellites, creating still more debris. In the worst case, certain orbits could become so dangerous that they would be unusable for generations, threatening services on which modern societies depend.

Several solutions are being explored. Engineers have tested nets, magnets and even harpoons designed to capture old satellites and drag them down into the atmosphere, where they burn up. New satellites are increasingly designed to leave orbit at the end of their working lives. Yet technology alone cannot solve the problem. Space is shared by many countries and companies, and no single authority has the power to enforce rules.

In this sense, the challenge resembles other problems involving shared resources, such as overfishing. Each user benefits from using the resource, while the costs of damage are spread among everyone. Unless nations find ways to cooperate, the space above our heads may become as polluted as the oceans below.

מאז שוגר הלוויין המלאכותי הראשון בשנות החמישים, שלחו בני האדם אלפי עצמים למסלול סביב כדור הארץ. לוויינים תומכים כיום בחיזוי מזג האוויר, בניווט, בתקשורת ובמחקר מדעי. אבל החלל סביב כוכב הלכת שלנו נעשה צפוף, וחלק גדול ממה שנמצא שם כבר אינו שימושי.

מומחים משתמשים במונח "פסולת חלל" כדי לתאר לוויינים מתים, חלקי טילים שהושלכו ואינספור שברים שנוצרים כאשר עצמים מתפרקים או מתנגשים. אפילו שבר זעיר עלול להיות מסוכן. מאחר שעצמים במסלול נעים במהירויות עצומות, מהר פי כמה מקליע, פיסת מתכת בגודל של מטבע יכולה לפגוע בעוצמה של פיצוץ. חלליות הנושאות אסטרונאוטים נאלצות לפעמים לשנות מסלול כדי להימנע משברים כאלה.

החשש הגדול ביותר הוא מתגובת שרשרת. אם שני עצמים גדולים מתנגשים, הם עלולים ליצור אלפי שברים חדשים, שכל אחד מהם עלול לפגוע בלוויינים אחרים וליצור פסולת נוספת. בתרחיש הגרוע ביותר, מסלולים מסוימים עלולים להפוך למסוכנים כל כך שלא יהיה ניתן להשתמש בהם במשך דורות, דבר שיאיים על שירותים שהחברה המודרנית תלויה בהם.

Most students prepare for exams by rereading their notes and highlighting key sentences. These methods feel productive: the material becomes familiar, and familiarity creates a pleasant sense of mastery. Unfortunately, research in cognitive psychology suggests that this feeling is often misleading.

In a typical experiment, two groups of students study the same text. One group reads it several times. The other reads it once and then tries to recall as much as possible without looking, writing down whatever they remember. Immediately afterwards, the rereading group usually feels more confident. A week later, however, the picture changes: the students who practised recalling the information remember considerably more.

Psychologists call this the 'testing effect', and it belongs to a broader set of findings sometimes described as 'desirable difficulties'. The idea is that learning which feels effortful tends to last longer. Spacing study sessions over several days rather than cramming the night before, mixing different types of problems instead of practising one type repeatedly, and explaining ideas in one's own words all make learning harder in the short term. Yet each of these strategies strengthens long-term memory.

Why should difficulty help? One explanation is that retrieving information from memory is not simply a way of checking what we know; it actively reorganises and reinforces that knowledge. Each successful act of recall makes the memory easier to find next time.

The findings have clear implications for teachers and learners. A classroom in which students are frequently asked to retrieve information, through low-pressure quizzes for example, may look less smooth than one in which the teacher simply presents material. But smoothness is not the goal. As one researcher put it, the sensation of learning and the reality of learning are not the same thing, and students who understand the difference are likely to study far more effectively.

רוב התלמידים מתכוננים למבחנים באמצעות קריאה חוזרת של הסיכומים שלהם וסימון משפטי מפתח. השיטות האלה מרגישות פרודוקטיביות: החומר נעשה מוכר, והמוּכרות יוצרת תחושה נעימה של שליטה. לרוע המזל, מחקרים בפסיכולוגיה קוגניטיבית מראים שהתחושה הזו מטעה לעתים קרובות.

בניסוי טיפוסי, שתי קבוצות של תלמידים לומדות את אותו טקסט. קבוצה אחת קוראת אותו כמה פעמים. השנייה קוראת אותו פעם אחת ואז מנסה להיזכר בכמה שיותר בלי להסתכל, ורושמת את כל מה שהיא זוכרת. מיד אחר כך, קבוצת הקריאה החוזרת מרגישה בדרך כלל בטוחה יותר. אולם כעבור שבוע התמונה משתנה: התלמידים שתרגלו שליפה של המידע זוכרים הרבה יותר.

פסיכולוגים מכנים זאת "אפקט הבחינה", והוא שייך לקבוצה רחבה יותר של ממצאים המתוארים לעתים כ"קשיים רצויים". הרעיון הוא שלמידה שמרגישה מאומצת נוטה להחזיק מעמד זמן רב יותר. פיזור מפגשי הלמידה על פני כמה ימים במקום לדחוס הכול בלילה שלפני, ערבוב של סוגי תרגילים שונים במקום לתרגל סוג אחד שוב ושוב, והסבר רעיונות במילים שלך, כל אלה מקשים על הלמידה בטווח הקצר. ובכל זאת, כל אחת מהאסטרטגיות האלה מחזקת את הזיכרון לטווח הארוך.

מדוע קושי אמור לעזור? הסבר אחד הוא ששליפת מידע מהזיכרון אינה רק דרך לבדוק מה אנו יודעים; היא מארגנת מחדש ומחזקת באופן פעיל את הידע הזה. כל פעולה מוצלחת של היזכרות מקלה על מציאת הזיכרון בפעם הבאה.

לממצאים יש השלכות ברורות על מורים ולומדים. כיתה שבה התלמידים מתבקשים לעתים קרובות לשלוף מידע, למשל באמצעות בחנים קצרים ללא לחץ, עשויה להיראות פחות חלקה מכיתה שבה המורה פשוט מציג את החומר. אבל חלקוּת אינה המטרה. כפי שניסח זאת אחד החוקרים, התחושה של למידה והמציאות של למידה אינן אותו דבר, ותלמידים שמבינים את ההבדל צפויים ללמוד ביעילות רבה הרבה יותר.
